overview.text: The Adrian helmet was a steel combat helmet adopted by France during World War I. The French War Ministry sought better protection after soldiers suffered numerous head wounds, and it approved quartermaster Adrian’s design in May 1915. Its recognizable raised crest ran along the top of a shell assembled from several pieces. A visor and rear neck guard helped cover parts of the head exposed in combat. The helmet also had a leather chinstrap, a blue-gray finish matching French uniforms, and a front badge identifying the wearer’s military branch. It became a distinctive image of French troops in the war.

key_facts.text: France approved Adrian’s helmet design on May 21, 1915.
The raised piece along the crown was called the crest.
Its front badge could identify a soldier’s branch of service.
The museum’s example bears an infantry grenade badge.
A June 1915 order called for 1.6 million helmets.

overview.text: Mycenaean civilization flourished on the Greek mainland during the Late Bronze Age, roughly 1600–1100 BCE. Its name comes from Mycenae, one of several fortified centers alongside places such as Tiryns and Pylos. Palace scribes used Linear B tablets to record an early form of Greek, providing direct evidence for administration and language. Mycenaean craftspeople made pottery, metalwork, and jewelry, while merchants carried goods across the Mediterranean. Their builders erected massive fortification walls and beehive-shaped tombs. Homer later placed Mycenae and other centers in his epics, but his stories are literature rather than proof that every legendary character existed. Many centers declined after destruction in the late thirteenth century BCE.

key_facts.text: Mycenaean culture dates approximately from 1600 to 1100 BCE.
Linear B tablets recorded an early Greek language.
Mycenae and Tiryns were important fortified centers.
Mycenaean pottery reached distant Mediterranean regions.
Late-thirteenth-century destruction preceded decline at many sites.

overview.text: The Bonfire of the Vanities was a public burning in Florence during Carnival in 1497, connected with the Dominican preacher Girolamo Savonarola. His reform movement urged Florentines to reject worldly display and change their customs. Objects condemned as “vanities” were placed in the fire; the precise losses of Renaissance artworks are difficult to establish, so claims about individual paintings require caution. The event shows how religious reform and political influence could shape public life in a Renaissance city. Savonarola’s relationship with images was complicated: he also used illustrated printed pamphlets to spread his sermons. The bonfire belongs to his brief period of strong influence in Florence.

key_facts.text: The famous Florentine bonfire took place during Carnival in 1497.
Girolamo Savonarola was a Dominican friar and preacher.
His reform program sought changes in Florentine customs.
The Metropolitan Museum says Renaissance artworks may have been destroyed; the extent is uncertain.
Savonarola also used images in printed pamphlets to communicate his message.

overview.text: The ABC Powers were Argentina, Brazil, and Chile, three South American states that offered mediation during a 1914 conflict between the United States and Mexico. Their diplomats met American and Mexican representatives at Niagara Falls, Ontario, beginning on May 20. The talks were entangled with Mexico’s revolution and the question of replacing Victoriano Huerta’s government. Delegates discussed a provisional government and possible routes to peace. “ABC” is simply the three countries’ initials, not the name of a permanent organization. The conference illustrates an early effort by Latin American governments to take a diplomatic role in a crisis involving their northern neighbors.

The mediation conference opened at Niagara Falls, Ontario, on May 20, 1914.
The United States and Mexican representatives attended the talks.
Chile’s minister missed the opening session but appeared in a later plenary meeting.
The negotiators discussed forming a provisional Mexican government.

overview.text: On January 7, 2015, gunmen attacked the Paris office of Charlie Hebdo, a French satirical magazine, during an editorial meeting. Twelve people were killed, including journalists and cartoonists, and others were wounded. The magazine had published satire about political and religious subjects, including depictions of Muhammad; this context was central to public discussion of the attack. The shooting prompted international condemnation and debates about freedom of expression, violence, and religious offense. Further violence occurred in France over the next two days, but the twelve deaths at Charlie Hebdo refer specifically to the magazine attack. The event became a prominent example of terrorism directed at journalists.

key_facts.text: The attack occurred in Paris on January 7, 2015.
Twelve people were killed at the Charlie Hebdo office.
Eight of those killed were journalists, according to UNESCO.
The magazine satirized politicians and religions, including publishing cartoons of Muhammad.
Connected attacks occurred in France on January 8 and 9.

overview.text: Operation Opera was an Israeli airstrike on Iraq’s Osirak nuclear reactor near Baghdad on June 7, 1981. Israeli aircraft flew to the site and destroyed the reactor. Israel presented the mission as a preventive action against what it feared Iraq might do with a nuclear program; that rationale is Israel’s stated position, not proof of an imminent Iraqi weapon. The strike raised a major international dispute over force against a nuclear facility. Iraq brought the attack before the United Nations Security Council. The raid is remembered for its long-distance flight and for the enduring debate over whether preventive attacks can be justified by uncertain future threats.

key_facts.text: Israeli aircraft struck Osirak on June 7, 1981.
The reactor was southeast of Baghdad.
Eight F-16s carried out the attack, with six F-15s assigned support roles.
The Israeli Defense Forces describe preventing a possible Iraqi nuclear threat as their rationale.
Iraq raised the raid at the UN Security Council in June 1981.

overview.text: The Conquest of the Desert was a series of late-nineteenth-century Argentine military campaigns to extend state control over Indigenous territories, especially toward Patagonia. General Julio Argentino Roca led a major campaign beginning in 1879. The name “desert” reflected a government viewpoint: Indigenous peoples already lived in these lands. Argentine forces took territory, and Indigenous communities experienced killing, captivity, displacement, and lasting loss of land. Photographs of the expedition include Indigenous captives, making the human consequences visible alongside official military records. The campaign helped reshape Argentina’s southern frontier, but its history is also a history of violence against the region’s existing peoples.

key_facts.text: Julio Argentino Roca led a major campaign that began in 1879.
The campaign expanded Argentine control over Indigenous lands.
Indigenous survivors experienced confinement or exile.
An official expedition photographer, Antonio Pozzo, recorded troops and captives.
The term “desert” obscures the fact that Indigenous communities lived there.

overview.text: A fortification is a structure or system built to make a place harder to attack. Across history, defenders have used earth banks, ditches, timber palisades, stone walls, towers, gates, and later works designed for artillery. These features serve different purposes: walls obstruct entry, towers improve observation and defense, and a gatehouse protects an otherwise vulnerable opening. A moat may be dry or water-filled. Medieval castles often combined several features instead of relying on one wall. Because weapons changed, fortifications changed too; defenses that suited archers were altered when guns and cannon became important. The term covers more than castles, including fortified towns and other defended sites.

key_facts.text: A fortification is designed to defend a place against attack.
Moats around castles could be dry or filled with water.
Gatehouses protected openings in castle walls.
Early medieval defenses often used earth and timber.
Later defenses adapted to the use of gunpowder weapons.

overview.text: Egyptian hieroglyphs were a formal writing system of ancient Egypt, often carved on monuments and sacred objects. Their pictures are meaningful signs, but they do not work as simple picture labels: some represent sounds, others words or ideas, and others help clarify meaning. Scribes also used hieratic, a more cursive script suited to writing with ink. Centuries after hieroglyphs fell out of regular use, scholars used the Rosetta Stone to reconnect the signs with language. That stone carried the same decree in hieroglyphic, demotic, and Greek writing. Jean-François Champollion’s 1822 breakthrough helped make ancient Egyptian texts readable again.

key_facts.text: Hieroglyphic signs can represent sounds, words, or meaning cues.
The Rosetta Stone presents a decree in hieroglyphic, demotic, and Greek scripts.
Jean-François Champollion made a major decipherment breakthrough in 1822.
Hieratic was a more cursive Egyptian script used with ink.
Hieroglyphs frequently appeared as carved monumental writing.

overview.text: Ferdinand Marcos governed the Philippines until the 1986 People Power Revolution ended his rule. He declared martial law in 1972, and a contemporary U.S. diplomatic report recorded arrests of opposition figures and journalists. One leading opponent, Senator Benigno “Ninoy” Aquino Jr., was assassinated in 1983 after returning to Manila; his death helped bring his widow Corazon Aquino into opposition leadership. A disputed 1986 snap election intensified protests. As crowds and defecting officials challenged Marcos, he and his family fled the country, and Corazon Aquino became president. Philippine institutions later pursued recovery of wealth alleged to have been acquired unlawfully by the Marcos family.

key_facts.text: A U.S. diplomatic report documented Marcos’s September 1972 martial-law declaration.
The report recorded arrests of opposition figures and journalists.
Benigno Aquino Jr. was assassinated after returning to the Philippines in August 1983.
The disputed February 1986 election preceded the People Power uprising.
The Marcos family fled to Hawaii as Corazon Aquino took power in 1986.
